:::

Full text

Abstract

Formula-fed infants have altered gut microbiota and immune development relative to breastfed infants. Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) and microbes able to ferment these, like Bifidobacterium infantis, promote healthy immune-microbiome interactions in breastfed infants.

In this randomized trial, 240 healthy term infants in the Philippines received a synbiotic formula (SynF; seven HMOs, bovine milk oligosaccharides, and B. infantis LMG11588) or control formula (CtrlF) for 6 months. SynF supported growth non-inferior to CtrlF and near universal B. infantis colonization (vs <10% in CtrlF). Markers of intestinal inflammation were lower in children fed SynF while secretory IgA was higher. SynF fed infants showed lower markers of systemic inflammation in plasma, slower immune cell maturation, and fewer upper respiratory tract infections (URTI) during their first 6 months of life. These findings suggest that synbiotic formula can dampen inflammatory responses to colonizing microbes and mild infections in fully formula-fed, term infants. Trial registration: NCT06073652.

Main

Breastfeeding is the gold standard for infant nutrition, providing substantial benefits that lead to a balanced development of the microbiota and immune system via early life immunemicrobiome interactions that promote long-term health 1 . Breast milk provides essential nutrients to the child but also a complex array of bioactive components, including human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), lactoferrin 2 and other bioactive proteins (e.g. immunoglobulins) 3 , as well as a diverse microbial community that collectively shape the infant gut microbiome and limit inflammatory responses to commensal microbes 4,5 . Breastfed infants harbor gut microbiomes dominated by infant-type Bifidobacterium species, particularly Bifidobacterium longum subsp. infantis, which has co-evolved with the mother-infant dyad to efficiently metabolize HMOs [6] [7] [8] . This bifidobacteria-dominant microbiome has been associated with reduced markers of gut inflammation, enhanced mucosal immune defenses upon infection and lower risks of allergic diseases, and metabolic disorders 8, 9 . However, despite strong recommendations for exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life, global breastfeeding rates remain suboptimal, with 30-40% of infants receiving infant formula either exclusively or as a supplement 1.

Formula-fed infants exhibit distinct gut microbiome profiles characterized by lower Bifidobacterium abundance, higher microbial diversity, and increased prevalence of potentially pathogenic taxa such as Clostridioides difficile and Ruminococcus gnavus 10, 11 . This altered microbiome composition has been associated with elevated gut inflammation, increased intestinal permeability, and a more activated systemic immune phenotype 12, 13 . A finding of particular concern is that recent studies have documented a generational decline in B. infantis colonization among infants in industrialized nations, which has been proposed as one potential contributor to the rising incidence of immune-mediated allergic and autoimmune diseases 8 . These observations have motivated efforts to develop infant formulas supplemented with bioactive components that can narrow the gap between formula-fed and breastfed infants.

Human milk oligosaccharides represent the third largest solid component of human milk, with concentrations ranging from 5-15 g/L 5,14 . These structurally diverse complex carbohydrates are indigestible by the infant and instead serve as selective substrates for beneficial gut bacteria, particularly B. infantis, which possess specialized enzymatic machinery to metabolize HMOs 6, 15.

Beyond their prebiotic function, HMOs exert direct immunomodulatory effects, serving as decoy receptors that prevent pathogen adhesion to epithelial cells and modulating immune cell responses 16, 17 . Advances in biotechnology have enabled the large-scale production of HMOs identical to those found in human milk, including 2'-fucosyllactose (2'FL), lacto-N-tetraose (LNT), lacto-N-neotetraose (LNnT), and sialylated oligosaccharides 18 . Clinical trials have demonstrated that infant formulas supplemented with one to six manufactured HMOs are safe, well-tolerated, and support normal growth, with some studies reporting stool microbiome shifts towards a more breastfed-like microbial composition and even reduced morbidity [19] [20] [21] [22].

Similarly, bovine milk-derived oligosaccharides (MOS or galacto-oligosaccharides) and probiotic Bifidobacterium strains have been evaluated as formula supplements 23 . MOS at concentrations up to 7.2 g/L have been shown to promote softer stools, increased fecal bifidobacteria abundances, and a shift in overall microbiota composition closer to that of breastfed infants 24 . Supplementation with B. infantis has demonstrated safety and tolerability in multiple trials, with evidence of persistent colonization, increased short-chain fatty acid production [25] [26] [27] , and modulation of fecal cytokine profiles suggestive of reduced enteric inflammation 8 . Although several studies have assessed probiotics, particularly supplementation with B. infantis, most of these have focused on additive effects in breastfed infants. It remains unknown whether synbiotic supplements benefit exclusively formula-fed infants, and no prior study has characterized local immune-microbiome interactions and systemic immune development in relation to nutritional interventions so early in life.

Here, we report results from a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial evaluating an infant formula supplemented with a synbiotic blend comprising seven human identical manufactured HMOs (2.64 g/L total), bovine milk oligosaccharides (4.56 g/L), and Bifidobacterium longum subsp. infantis LMG11588 (10⁶ CFU/g) in term-born, formula-fed infants. The HMO concentrations in this formula fall within the range observed in mature human milk 12 . The primary objective was to demonstrate non-inferior growth compared with a standard infant formula at 4 months of age. Predefined secondary objectives included assessment of safety, gastrointestinal tolerance, gut microbiome composition, and fecal biomarkers of gut health. In a pre-specified sub-study, we performed comprehensive systemic immune profiling using mass cytometry, multidimensional plasma protein profiling, and vaccine response assays to characterize how synbiotic supplementation affects immune-microbiome interactions and systemic immune maturation during the first six months after birth. We further examined associations between gut microbiome developmental trajectories, stool metabolites, and systemic immune markers. Our findings demonstrate that synbiotic formula promotes a coordinated maturation of the gut-microbiome with a dominance of bifidobacteria, reduced markers of inflammation in the gut and in systemic circulation, and fewer and shorter episodes of symptomatic respiratory infections. Together, these outcomes are consistent with a real-world illustration of a more balanced immune states and a more regulated inflammatory set point early in life.

Results

Study infants and baseline characteristics

A total of 243 infants in Manila, the Philippines were screened and 240 were randomized into the CtrlF (n=122) and SynF (n=118) groups forming the Intention-To-Treat (ITT) dataset (Fig. 1a).

Seventeen infants were excluded from the Full Analysis Set (FAS) as they did not receive any study product, leaving 114 and 109 in the CtrlF and SynF groups, respectively. After excluding infants with major protocol deviations, 113 in the CtrlF group and 108 in the SynF group comprised the Per-Protocol (PP) population (Fig. 1a). For the blood sample analysis, N=43 and N=42 infants representative of CtrlF and SynF infants respectively were selected as Biomarker Analysis Set (BAS) (Fig. 1a). One additional SynF infant, sampled at baseline but not part of the FAS, contributes to the baseline blood measurements only (n=43 SynF infants at baseline in Fig. 5c and 5f). A total of 217 (90%) enrolled infants completed the study. Infant baseline demographic and household characteristics for the ITT and BAS were similar for SynF and CtrlF groups (Fig. 1b). These are consistent with the Full-Analysis Set (FAS) population and patients were monitored for 6 months and blood sampled at baseline, and 2-and 4-months while stool was collected at baseline, 2-, 4-and 6 months of life (Fig. 1c).

Anthropometrics

Weight gain velocity was non-inferior in the SynF group compared to the CtrlF group in the FAS and PP populations with a mean difference (95% CI) of 1.01 (-0.67, 2.68) (p<0.001). Weight gain velocity mean from baseline to 4 months was (95% CI) 28.0 (26.7, 29.3) and 27.0 (25.7, 28.3) g/day for the SynF (n=107) and the CtrlF (n=110) groups, respectively, in both FAS and PP datasets. No significant differences were observed between groups in weight-for-age, length-forage, weight-for-length, or head circumference-for-age z-scores at any time point and all were within normal range (Fig. 2a-d).

Gastrointestinal tolerance

Any nutritional intervention can be associated with intestinal discomfort in young children. We assessed Infant Gastrointestinal Symptom Questionnaire, IGSQ scores 28 and mean levels were low (≤18.0) in both groups over time, indicating good GI tolerance (Fig. 2e). Consistent with these findings, parent-reported stooling patterns from the 3-day diary showed that stools were slightly more frequent among SynF fed infants compared with CtrlF fed infants at months 3 (mean 2.0 vs 1.6; p=0.0457), 4 (mean 1.9 vs 1.4; p=0.0014), and 6 (mean 1.8 vs 1.5; p=0.0254).

Stools were also generally softer among SynF fed infants at months 1.5 (1.8 vs 2.0; p=0.0002), 2 (1.8 vs 2; p=0.0006), and 4 (1.8 vs 2; p=0.0013) compared to CtrlF fed infants though mean consistency in both groups was 'mushy-soft.' The number of days on which infants had difficulty passing stools was low and similar in both groups (all p>0.05).

Safety and exploratory efficacy

Adverse Events, AE incidence was similar in both groups (51.4% and 53.5% in SynF and CtrlF, respectively) (Table 1). Eight Serious Adverse Events, SAEs were reported (4 events in 4 infants per group), including one fatal event unrelated to the study in the CtrlF group (aspiration pneumonia). The number of infection-related AEs was similar in both groups (n=43 in SynF and n=48 in CtrlF). Fewer URTI events were reported among infants in the SynF group compared to those in the CtrlF group (19 vs 41 events of the MedDRA term upper respiratory tract infection, respectively; p=0.009; 25 vs 46 when viral URTI is included, p=0.023) (Table 2).

167

Intestinal barrier and immune biomarkers 168 SynF compared to CtrlF formula feeding was associated with reduced inflammatory biomarkers 169 in stool samples, including lower levels of calprotectin at 4 months, and alpha-1-antitrypsin, AAT 170 at 2, 4, and 6 months (all p<0.05) (Fig. 3a-b). This indicates a less inflammatory response to 171 colonizing microbes in SynF fed infants. Secretory IgA, sIgA in stool reflects an intestinal 172 immune system that is engaging with colonizing microbiota in a controlled, non-inflammatory 173 way, rather than one that is either immunologically naive or actively inflamed 29 . In breastfed 174 infants, sIgA is provided via breastmilk and partly explains the protective effect of breastmilk 175 from the catastrophic intestinal inflammation in necrotizing enterocolitis, NEC in preterms 30 . In 176 formula-fed infants, all sIgA is produced by the host and translocated via the polymeric Ig 177 receptor, pIgR 29 . At 4 months, the level of sIgA was higher in SynF vs CtrlF infants (p=0.0341) (Fig. 3c). Another biomarker of immune-microbiome interactions early in life is fecal pH which reflect the fermentation chemistry of gut microbes with lower pH in breastfed than formula fed infants 31 and among breastfed infants, pH is lower when the relative abundance of Bifidobacteria is higher 32 . We found that fecal pH was consistently lower in SynF compared to the CtrlF group from 2-6 months (p<0.0001) as another example of the synbiotic formula providing a more breastfed-like state as compared to control formula (Fig. 3d).

Gut microbiome development and metabolites

Microbiome diversity was assessed using alpha-diversity metrics (Richness, Shannon index, and Faith's phylogenetic diversity [Faith's PD]) and beta-diversity metrics (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and weighted UniFrac distance) and differed between SynF and CtrlF groups (p<0.0001) from 2-6 months (Fig. 4a). Low intra-individual (alpha-) diversity is generally observed in breastfed infants because of the dominance of Bifidobacterium species able to ferment HMOs. We measured bifidobacterium species by metagenomic sequencing and found higher abundances (mainly B. infantis, B. breve, B. longum, B. bifidum) from 2-6 months of age, both in relative (data not shown) and absolute terms (Fig. 4b). B. infantis dominated in SynF fed infants and showed the strongest increase over time (p<0.0001) (Fig. 4b). From 2 months, B. infantis (probiotic LMG11588 and endogenous strains) prevalences were virtually 100% in SynF fed infants, while most CtrlF fed infants had barely detectable B. infantis through their first 6 months (Fig. 4b). Infants born via C-section and without older siblings showed the strongest bifidobacteria increase in SynF compared to CtrlF fed infants from 2-6 months (Supplementary Fig. 1a-b). As expected from the strong increase in infant-type bifidobacteria, an increase in internal HMO utilization capacity is seen in the SynF group from 2 to 6 months: GH95, GH29 for fucosylated HMOs; GH33 for sialylated HMOs; GH42, GH112 for type-1 core structures and GH20 (Fig. 4c). The CtrlF formula fed infants showed higher levels of secreted GH95, GH29, GH136 and GH2 at 6 months. The SynF group is characterized by high relative (and absolute) abundance of infant type bifidobacteria, the CtrlF group has higher relative abundance of other taxa that generally colonize to higher abundances, later, after 6 months. Among those, the mucosal glycan forager Ruminococcus gnavus was higher in CtrlF vs SynF fed infants from 2-6 months (Fig. 4b). All in all, these results show that feeding synbiotic formula containing HMO, BMO, and probiotic Bifidobacterium infantis strongly impacts gut microbiome development in favor of the probiotic strain and other HMO metabolizing microbes commonly seen in breastfed infants.

Microbial metabolites in relation to formula feeding

Metabolites produced by microbes are known to exert immunomodulatory effects and contribute to the establishment of healthy immune-microbiome interactions early in life 33 . For example, we previously found that indole-3 lactic acid (ILA), a tryptophan metabolite was associated with lower levels of intestinal inflammation and immunomodulation in breastfed infants fed probiotic B. infantis 8 . In the formula-fed infants studied here we also found that ILA in stool was positively correlated with B. infantis and B. bifidum abundances and strongly associated with SynF feeding between 2-6 months (Fig. 4d). Short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are another class of metabolites known to exert beneficial effects on epithelial cells and developing immune cells early in life 33 . SCFA acetate is associated with breastfeeding and the presence of HMO metabolizing bifidobacteria 34 , and acetate has been associated with reduced risks of allergy, months, like ILA (Fig. 4d). Butyrate has also been associated with reduced risks of immune mediated disease, but butyrate is usually a product of clostridial colonization later in infancy and in SynF children we found an inverse correlation between butyrate and B. infantis abundances (Fig. 4d). A similar pattern was seen for propionate levels (Supplementary Fig. 2). These findings indicate that synbiotic formula retains a developing microbiome in a B. infantis, acetate and ILA dominated state, characteristic of the intestinal milieu of exclusively breastfed 8 and associated with favorable immune-microbiome interactions in contrast to the accelerated maturation upon early weaning (<3 months) associated with increased risks of immune-mediated disease 36.

Systemic immune profile development

To directly assess the effects of CtrlF vs SynF on immune development we performed systemslevel analyses of longitudinal whole blood samples collected at baseline, and at 2-and 4 months within the BAS population. Mass cytometry analysis of 21,865,760 whole blood cells was manually classified by known marker combinations into 27 core immune cell populations (Supplementary Fig. 3). Principal component analysis of immune cell frequencies showed that overall immune cell composition is structured by age (Fig. 5a, b), and that the cells increasing after birth are B cells, neutrophils, and CD8 + T effector cells, while the cells decreasing in blood after birth are classical monocytes, regulatory T cells, and central memory CD4 + T cells 37 , possibly reflecting gut homing of these cells 8 (Supplementary Fig. 4). Using pseudotime 38 derived from the top time-varying cell populations as an integrated readout of immune cell maturation, SynF and CtrlF infants were indistinguishable at baseline (d = 0.12, p = 0.943) and at 2 months (d = -0.08, p = 0.628), but trended lower in SynF by 4 months (d = -0.46, p = 0.057) suggestive of a slightly slower maturation of immune cells in blood in children fed synbiotic 248 formula (Fig. 5c). 249 250.

Plasma protein profiling 39 (Olink Explore 384 Inflammation I) revealed a reproducible pattern in which markers of immune activation and chemotaxis, including KLRB1, CD160, TNFSF10, FASLG, GZMA, IL12RB1, CD70, CD6, LY9, LAMP3, CTSO, CCL3, CCL4, JUN, PLAUR and SCGN, increased less from baseline in SynF than in CtrlF infants at 2 months and 4 months (smaller change in SynF for all 16; nominal p < 0.05 for 13 of 16 at 4 months and 7 of 16 at 2 months, at both timepoints for CD6, CD70, PLAUR and SCGN; none significant after FDR correction) (Fig. 5d). The consistency of an attenuated-activation pattern across timepoints and among proteins with overlapping functions (cytotoxic/effector lymphocyte activation and inflammatory chemotaxis) indicate dampened inflammatory responses in SynF vs CtrlF feeding in this cohort, even when individual markers remain nominally significant only.

To test whether a coordinated biological process associated with feeding mode could be identified, we constructed a joint co-regulation network combining the 27 immune cell population frequencies (CLR-transformed) and all 358 Olink proteins (log2 NPX), using weighted gene co-regulation network analysis (WGCNA) 40 . This identified six co-regulation modules (Fig. 5e), numbered by size. Module 3 (40 features: CD8 + T central-memory, effectormemory, and TEMRA populations, together with 37 Olink proteins) captured a coherent CD8 + effector/memory T cell axis, including 7 of the 16 proteins highlighted above (KLRB1, CD160, TNFSF10, IL12RB1, FASLG, GZMA, LAMP3). Pairwise correlations among Module 3 features were substantially stronger than background (median bicor 0.43 vs 0.11 across the rest of the network), confirming these markers represent a coordinated biological unit during immune development. The Module 3 eigengene did not differ between feeding groups at baseline (Cohen's d=0.25, p=0.368) or 2 months (d=0.05, p=0.879) but was significantly lower in SynF at 4 months (d=-0.44, p=0.027) (Fig. 5f). Collectively, these findings are consistent with SynF feeding promoting a modestly slower immune maturation trajectory, and more regulated immune activation both at the intestinal mucosa and in circulation.

Vaccine antibody responses

To assess the impact of CtrlF vs SynF feeding on vaccine immunogenicity, we measured IgG antibodies against 36 vaccine-related antigens at 4 months. Vaccine-specific IgG responses did not differ meaningfully between feeding groups and none of the 36 antigens reached FDR significance (Supplementary Fig. 5). Four antigens showed nominally higher levels in CtrlF (p<0.05), but all antigens were from the Measles/Mumps/Rubella, MMR vaccine (measles nucleoprotein, rubella E1, native measles, mumps nucleoprotein) and these vaccines were not administered until the age of nine months. These antibodies therefore likely represent maternal antibodies transferred during pregnancy 41 , and higher levels at 4 months could reflect increased FcRn-mediated IgG recycling associated with systemic inflammation in CtrlF 42.

Trajectories of gut microbiome colonization track with intestinal inflammation

To go beyond individual microbe abundances and metrics of microbial diversity, we inferred Fecal Community Type (FCT) trajectories 43 . Four FCTs described trajectories (Fig. 6a) and FCTs were strongly associated with feeding group (Fig. 6b). CtrlF fed infants were predominantly assigned to trajectories T1 and T4, while SynF fed infants were predominantly assigned to trajectories T2 and T3, the latter characterized by early and sustained bifidobacterium dominance (data not shown). FCT trajectory was also associated with fecal markers of intestinal inflammation and barrier function across visits (Fig. 6c). Fecal pH differed most consistently and strongly between trajectories at every timepoint, secretory IgA showed trajectory-associated 297 differences that shifted in magnitude and direction over time, and the antitrypsin-related 298 measures showed more timepoint-specific differences, most prominent from 2 to 4 months. 299

Together with the feeding-group associations in Fig. 6a and b, this supports gut microbial 300 community trajectory as a route through which SynF feeding shapes the local intestinal 301 environment and dampen inflammatory responses early in life. 302

Respiratory tract infections in relation to feeding groups

An increased propensity to respond with strong inflammatory responses upon infection has been linked to immune-microbiome interactions at mucosal surfaces, particularly in the airways [44] [45] [46] [47].

To assess the effects of formula feeding mode and immune development on real-world consequences for health, we tracked episodes of upper respiratory infections (URTI) in infants fed CtrlF and SynF (Fig. 7a-b). We observed fewer episodes of URTI events in SynF vs CtrlF (Poisson regression, p=0.023) and lower Incidence Rate Ratios, IRR per child year in SynF vs CtrlF (IRR=0.586; 95% CI: 0.356, 0.954; p=0.023) corresponding to a 41% reduction in event rates (Fig. 7c). The duration of symptomatic infections is an indication of severity and linked to overall immune regulation. In this study, we found a trend towards shorter duration of first URTI in the SynF group compared to CtrlF (p=0.07)(Fig. 7d). These findings point towards a realworld consequence of a more tempered immune development and immune-microbe interactions less prone to drive inflammatory responses may be fewer symptomatic infections. Given that such infections have been linked to risks of immune mediated diseases such as asthma and wheeze, future trials with longer follow-up will be required to investigate whether synbiotic formula feeding and dampened inflammatory responses could prevent immune mediated disease.

Discussion

This randomized, double-blind, controlled trial demonstrates that a synbiotic infant formula combining seven HMOs, BMOs, and B. infantis LMG11588 supports non-inferior growth, while promoting healthier microbiome and immune development. The prespecified primary and secondary outcomes for which the study was powered, converge on a coherent biological narrative, that synbiotic supplementation promotes a bifidobacterium-dominant gut microbiome which tempers inflammatory signaling both systemically and at mucosal sites, without compromising vaccine immunogenicity or infant health.

The primary and prespecified endpoint for this trial was growth (defined by weight gain velocity) non-inferiority, and our findings replicate the consistent safety signal seen in prior trials of the same probiotic strain 32 and HMO supplementation trials [19] [20] [21] . What distinguishes this trial is the use of a synbiotic formulation and the deep analyses of microbiome composition, microbial metabolites, markers of intestinal health, and systems-level analyses of immune development in longitudinal blood samples. The results show robust B. infantis colonization in infants fed SynF as compared to CtrlF (approaching 100% vs <10%), exceeding what has been reported previously for probiotic or prebiotic interventions in formula-fed infants 48 . This also parallels our prior work in breastfed infants supplemented with B. infantis, which demonstrated that B. infantis colonization and HMO fermentation robustly correlated with increased tryptophan metabolites in general, and indole-3-lactic acid (ILA), in particular as a key immunomodulatory metabolite 8 , a finding replicated here in fully formula-fed infants. This result also suggests a mechanistic pathway for the observed beneficial effects whereby Bifidobacterium-dependent tryptophan fermentation leads to dampened inflammatory responses against colonizing microbes.

In addition, the fecal markers of inflammation calprotectin and α-1-antitrypsin were lower whereas the secretory IgA produced by infants themselves in the absence of breastmilk was higher, indicating a less inflammatory gut environment and a healthier mucosal barrier in the gut.

The longitudinal effects on systemic immune development herein have not been reported previously in exclusively formula-fed infants. The observation that gut microbial community evolution tracked with feeding group, and with markers of intestinal inflammation, is mechanistically informative and consistent with a model in which immune-and barrier-related changes are mediated through effects on colonizing microbes rather than direct effects of formula components on immunity. Unsupervised network analysis (WGCNA) integrating the cell and protein data independently converged on a CD8⁺ T effector/memory axis as a coregulated module (rather than a set of coincidental cell and protein hits) that was lower in SynF infants by 4 months after birth, lending additional support to a synbiotic-associated tempering of systemic immune activation and dampened inflammatory responses to commensal microbes. The finding of fewer URTI episodes and a trend towards a shorter duration of URTIs in the SynF group provides evidence that the immunological changes we observed may translate the optimized immune-microbiome interactions into a real-world health outcome of clinical relevance. This is also in line with data from a preclinical mouse model 49 . Mechanistically, it is tempting to speculate that rates of infection did not differ between groups but that inflammatory responses to colonizing microbes in the gut and perhaps also in the airways, leads to more balanced responses also upon viral infections and potentially also other environmental exposures such as food components, vaccines, and environmental chemicals, with less inflammation and tissue damage as a result. Future studies will be required to test this hypothesis directly and assess possible protection from immune mediated diseases such as asthma and allergy.

Several limitations deserve consideration. The trial was conducted exclusively in metropolitan Manila, the Philippines, in families who had independently elected not to breastfeed prior to enrollment. This appropriately restricts the trial to infants for whom formula feeding is the established nutritional mode but precludes an internal breastfed comparator arm. The degree of bridging achieved by the synbiotic formula can therefore only be inferred from the biomarker literature. The immune sub-study enrolled 86 of 240 infants on a first-come, first-served basis with possible selection bias. Mass cytometry and Olink findings are best considered exploratory as the large number of immune parameters evaluated means that independent replication is required for validation purposes. It is also important to understand how the same interventions replicate their effects across different ethnic populations and different environmental contexts, given the importance of microbial and other environmental exposures on immune variation in humans 50 . The URTI outcome was captured as an adverse event rather than a pre-specified primary endpoint, making it susceptible to differential ascertainment and recall bias across sites and visits. The trial was not powered to detect subgroup-specific effects, and therefore the stronger Bifidobacterium enrichment in C-section-born and sibling-free SynF fed infants, while biologically plausible, is exploratory. Additionally, the multi-component synbiotic design precludes disentangling the individual contributions of HMOs, bovine MOS, and B. infantis, a limitation that would require additional factorial or dose-finding trials to address, although several previous trials have been conducted on some of these components already. This trial demonstrates effects on growth, colonization, biomarkers, and exploratory immune measurements but does not establish any associations with long-term protection against allergy, infection, or immune-mediated disease and that remains to be tested?

The trial was conducted in a predominantly urban Philippine cohort with high rates of cesarean delivery and very low baseline B. infantis colonization among CtrlF fed infants (<10%). This baseline colonization ecology resembles the current situation in many high-income countries where generational depletion of B. infantis has occurred [51] [52] [53] , suggesting that the dramatic colonization effect is likely reproducible in such settings, but perhaps not in settings where baseline colonization is higher. However, differences in microbiome background, infection pressure, antibiotic exposure, and vaccine schedules across countries are likely to modulate the immunological effects observed, and findings cannot be assumed to generalize uniformly.

The restriction to term infants whose parents elected not to breastfeed means these findings do not extend to preterm or low birth weight populations, to mixed-fed infants, or to settings where breastfeeding is supplemented or discontinued for medical reasons. The 6-month observation window, while sufficient to characterize microbiome and immune development during the most dynamic period, does not allow conclusions about the durability of the immune phenotype after formula cessation or dietary diversification. Whether the dampened inflammatory trajectory translates into measurable reductions in atopic disease, autoimmunity, or metabolic outcomes in later childhood remains an important open question requiring extended follow-up.

In summary, this trial provides multi-modal evidence that a complex synbiotic formula can substantially recapitulate key features of the breastfed gut-immune axis in formula-fed term infants. The convergent evidence from microbiome sequencing, metabolomics, mucosal biomarkers, and systems-level immunomonitoring provides insights beyond what any single modality could establish. Future trials should prioritize replication in geographically diverse cohorts, pre-specified clinical endpoints for additional real-world health outcomes such as infections and atopic outcomes, and longer follow-up to determine whether early-life immune programming by synbiotic formula has lasting consequences for child health.

Methods

Study design and population

In this randomized, double-blind, controlled intervention study (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06073652), infants were recruited from 3 medical centers in the metropolitan Manila (Philippines) area between August 2023 and February 2024. Infants aged ≥14 to ≤35 days were enrolled if they met the following inclusion criteria: healthy term infant (≥37 weeks of gestation); birth weight ≥2500g and ≤4500g; and at the time of enrollment, infants were exclusively consuming and tolerating a cow's milk infant formula and their parents have independently elected not to breastfeed before enrollment. Infants were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: evidence of feeding difficulties or formula intolerance such as vomiting or poor intake (investigator's discretion); have conditions requiring infant feedings besides those specified in the protocol; have conditions or medical history that could interfere with the study conduct and interpretation such as major congenital malformations, suspected or documented systemic or congenital infections, or previous or ongoing severe medical or laboratory abnormality that could affect study participation; presently received or have received prior to enrollment medication(s) or supplement(s) which are known or suspected to affect fat digestion, absorption and/or metabolism, stool microbiota and characteristics, growth, or gastric acid secretion; and currently participating or have participated in another interventional clinical trial since birth. No changes were made to the trial methods, including design, eligibility criteria, or pre-specified outcomes after trial commencement.

Ethics details

Randomization procedure and blinding

The infants who met the eligibility criteria were randomized to receive the synbiotic formula (SynF) or the control formula (CtrlF) in a 1:1 allocation ratio using the Medidata Randomization Trial Supply Management (New York, United States) with the dynamic allocation algorithm. The randomization was stratified by sex (female/male), center, and mode of delivery (vaginal/caesarean). Participants, parents/LAR(s), care providers at study sites, clinical investigators, laboratory personnel, data analysts, and sponsor personnel were all blinded to group assignments for the duration of the study. The randomization sequence was generated centrally by an independent biostatistician at Nestlé prior to study start and held within the Medidata RTSM. Study site investigators confirmed participant eligibility and formally enrolled each infant into the RTSM, which then automatically released the allocated formula code. No site personnel had access to the allocation sequence. The synbiotic and control formulas were identical in appearance, color, smell, packaging format, and labeling; labels indicated only the individualized product code, age range, and that the product was for clinical trial use, with no indication of group assignment.

Intervention and study products

Infants began their intervention at V1 (baseline, 14-35 days after birth) and continued through V6 (6 months of postnatal age), with additional clinic visits at V2 (1.5 months), V3 (2 months), V4 (3 months), and V5 (4 months). The synbiotic formula (SynF) contained a standard bovinemilk based term infant formula with 13.4 g/L protein composed of 65% intact whey protein: 35% casein protein ratio, 100% lactose, and a fat blend containing 45% high palmitate in the sn-2 position with the remaining fat component composed of soy oil, sunflower oil and coconut oil.

Additionally, the SynF was supplemented with a synbiotic blend which included 2.66 g/L of 7 manufactured HMOs (2'FL, 3FL, DFL, LNT, LNnT, 3'SL, 6'SL), 4.55 g/L bovine milk derived oligosaccharides (MOS; source of 3'GL, 4'GL, 6'GL), and 1x10^6 colony forming units (CFU) B. infantis (LMG11588) per gram formula powder. The control formula (CtrlF) group received the same formula as SynF except without the synbiotic blend (lactose was increased to compensate for the lack of HMOs and MOS). All study products were produced by Wyeth Nutritionals Ireland Ltd. (Askteaton, Co Limerick, Ireland) and provided in 400g cans and were fed orally, ad libitum, with amounts varying based on age, developmental stage, and appetite.

Although the formula intervention ended at V6 (6 months of age), parents/LARs were invited to complete an infant illness questionnaire every 6 months until age 36 months. The trial was completed as planned. Recruitment ended after the pre-specified sample size had been enrolled; no, early stopping rules were triggered. This follow-up phase is still ongoing as of the date of finalization of this manuscript and these results will be published separately.

Growth

Anthropometric measurements including weight (g), length (cm), and head circumference (cm) were collected using standardized procedures at V1 (baseline) through V6 (6 months). Weight gain measured as mean daily weight gain in g/day from V1 (baseline) to V5 (4 months) was the primary endpoint. Corresponding z-scores including weight-for-age, length-for-age, weight-forlength, and head-circumference-for-age were determined using the World Health Organization growth standards as the reference.

Gastrointestinal tolerance

Gastrointestinal (GI) tolerance, symptoms, and related behaviors were examined using the GI Symptom and Behavior Diary and the Infant Gastrointestinal Symptom Questionnaire (IGSQ) 28 , a validated, standardized questionnaire with 13 items across 5 domains (crying, stooling, flatulence, fussiness, and vomiting/spitting up) 28 . Stool frequency and consistency and GI symptoms and related behaviors were recorded in the retrospective 1-day record at V1 (baseline) and prospective 3-day GI Symptom and Behavior Diary for 3 days prior to V2 (1.5 months), V3 (2 months), V4 (3 months), V5 (4 months), and V6 (6 months). Stool frequency (mean number of stools), stool consistency (mean score;1=watery,2=runny,3=mushy/soft,4=firm,5=hard), GI symptoms including frequency and amount of spitting up/vomiting and flatulence, and GI-related behaviors such as crying, fussiness, and sleeping were captured in this diary. Additionally, the IGSQ was administered at V1 (baseline) and at V2 (1.5 months), V3 (2 months), V4 (3 months), V5 (4 months), and V6 (6 months) to derive a composite measure of GI symptom burden. A composite index score ranging from 13-65 was calculated by summing the domain scores, with lower scores representing a lower GI burden, so a score of 13-23 is considered indicative of good GI tolerance, a score of 24-30 indicates some GI distress, and scores above 30 are considered to reflect clinically meaningful GI symptom burden.

Biological sample collection

Fecal samples were collected at home by the parent(s)/LAR(s) at V1 (baseline) after the actual visit but prior to start of product intake and on any of the three days prior to V3 (2 months), V5 (4 months), and V6 (6 months). The parent(s)/LAR(s) received collection kits and a manual instructing them how to collect, store, and transport the samples. Once the fecal samples were brought to the study site, they were kept frozen at -80°C until analysis. Blood samples were collected by a medical technologist using the appropriate equipment (e.g., microneedles) for infant blood sampling and/or according to the site's standard of care. Samples of approximately 0.5-1.0 ml were collected at V1 (baseline), V3 (2 months), and V5 (4 months) in a subset of about 40 infants/randomized group on a first come, first serve principle so the first 40 parent(s)/LAR(s) in the SynF and CtrlF groups, respectively, to provide the optional consent for blood sample were included.

Fecal microbiota analysis

Fecal microbiota composition was assessed using shotgun metagenomics as described 22 , with minor modifications. Briefly, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was extracted from the fecal samples using the NucleoSpin Stool kit (Machery-Nagel) with bead beating at 2700 rpm for 5 min. DNA libraries were prepared using the Watchmaker DNA Library Prep Kit (7K0019-1K). Genomic DNA was fragmented using a mastermix of Watchmaker Frag/AT Buffer and Frag/AT Enzyme Mix. IDT xGen UDI Primers and IDT Stubby Adapters were added to each sample followed by 7 cycles of PCR to construct the DNA libraries. The final DNA libraries were purified using CleanNGS magnetic beads (CleanNA) and eluted in nuclease-free water. Following elution, the libraries were quantified using the Qubit™ fluorometer dsDNA HS Assay Kit and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X platform at 2x150bp. After removal of adapter and human DNA, fecal microbiota composition and diversity metrics were determined using CHAMP 54 . Gut Metabolic Modules were annotated based on species-level KO annotations, assigning a GMM if it included at least 2/3 of the KOs needed to complete the functionality of the module 55 . For modules with multiple reaction paths, only one path was required to be 2/3 complete and for modules with less than four steps, all steps were required to be comprised in the given species. GMM abundance was calculated as the summed abundance of all species annotated with a given module. HMOspecific glycosyl hydrolase (GH) families were annotated using run_dbcan (v. 3.0.2) 56 , retaining annotations that were identified by both HMMER (E < 1e-15, coverage > 0.5) and DIAMOND (E < 1e-100). Each GH gene was classified as "secreted" if a signal peptide was detected by DeepSig (v. 1.2.5) 57 , or "internal" if no signal peptide was detected.

Microbiota diversity indices were calculated from rarefied species abundances using richness, Faith's Phylogenetic Distance, and Shannon index as well as Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, and weighted UniFrac. Microbiome differences between the feeding groups were assessed using models correcting for site and baseline age using a linear regression framework with logtransformed relative abundances and a compositional bias correction based on LinDA 58.

Fecal community types (FCT) were determined using Dirichlet Multinominal Mixture (DMM) 43 at genus level with a prevalence filtering of >5% of samples and abundance filtering of >0.001% relative abundance. DMM models were run fitting from 1 to 10 clusters over 10 iterations using Laplace approximation to evaluate the optimal number of clusters. After an initial evaluation of five clusters that resulted in two being very similar, the model was constrained to four clusters. Individual subject trajectories of FCTs were established using state composition clustering. Other methods like Optimal Matching clustering were evaluated and dismissed due to the lack of a reference group. State Composition Clustering was done by summarizing each subject by the proportion of visits spent in each FCT state, computation of Manhattan distances between subjects on these proportions, and application of PAM (k-medoids) clustering. The optimal number of clusters was chosen based on Silhouette, Within-cluster sum of squares (WSS), and Gap statistics. Based on those three quality control measures, four trajectory clusters were identified as an optimal number.

Fecal metabolic profile and markers of gut immune health and gut barrier function

Fecal pH was assessed using a pH meter (Orion, Thermo Scientific, USA). Fecal D-and Llactate, D-and L-indole-lactate were measured by liquid chromatography coupled with a mass spectrometer (Acquity I-class UPLC Xevo TQ-XS system, Waters, USA). Briefly, fecal samples were weighed before and after lyophilization, and homogenized in orthophosphoric acid, followed by centrifugation to remove particulate matter. Supernatants were analyzed using LC-MS with separation of D/L-indole-3-lactic acid enantiomers using an Astec Chirobiotic R chiral column under a gentle gradient. Detection was carried out using a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer equipped with UniSpray TM source technology operating in multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). Quantification of the 2 enantiomers was performed using internal calibration methodology 59 . Fecal short and branched chain fatty acids (propionate, butyrate, acetate, valerate, iso-butyrate, 2-methylbutyrate, iso-valerate) were measured by gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometer (Agilent Technologies, USA) after deproteinization with 5sulfosalicylic acid, chloroform extraction and derivatization with tertbutyldimethylsilylimidazole. Selectivity and detection were carried out on a single quadrupole mass spectrometer, followed by integration of chromatographic peaks with Openlab CDS3 (Agilent, USA) and data quantification on Slims (Agilent, USA). Fecal secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA, kit #K8870), calprotectin (kit #K6967, and α-1antitrypsin (AAT, kit #K6750) were assessed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (Immundiagnostik AG, Bensheim, Germany) according to manufacturers' instructions.

Amounts of organic acids and protein markers were corrected per dry fecal weight and not per wet fecal weight as SynF had slightly softer stool.

Blood sample processing

Blood was drawn into K2EDTA tubes and processed within 2 hours of collection. For immune cell analysis, 0.4 mL of whole blood was mixed 1:1 with a proprietary stabilizer (Cytodelics AB, Stockholm, Sweden) 60 to preserve cell surface marker integrity. Plasma was separated by centrifugation and aliquoted (50 µL) for proteomic and antibody analyses. All samples were stored at -80°C and shipped on dry ice for centralized analysis.

Whole blood analyses by mass cytometry (CyTOF)

Cryopreserved stabilized whole blood samples 60 were thawed, fixed, and red blood cells were lysed according to the manufacturer's protocol (Cytodelics AB). Cells were barcoded using the Cell-ID 20-Plex Barcoding Kit (Standard BioTools Inc., South San Francisco, CA) with an automated liquid handling system 61 (Agilent Technologies) and pooled for batch staining. Cells were stained with a panel of >60 metal-conjugated antibodies targeting major immune cell lineages and functional subsets (Supplementary Table 2). Data were acquired on a CyTOF XT mass cytometer (Standard BioTools Inc.) at 300-500 cells/second using CyTOF software version 8.0. Raw data were normalized to calibration bead signals, arcsin h-transformed (co-factor 5), and batch-corrected using the ComBat algorithm (sva package in R). A manual gating strategy based on canonical marker combinations was used to define 28 core immune cell populations directly from the same normalized, batch-corrected data (Supplementary Fig. 3); this manually gated population set (27 populations after excluding one compositionally redundant population) was used for the primary cross-sectional and change-from-baseline population-frequency comparisons.

Plasma proteomics (Olink Explore)

Plasma protein profiling was performed using the Olink Explore 384 Inflammation I Panel (Olink Proteomics, Uppsala, Sweden), which quantifies 384 inflammation-related proteins using Proximity Extension Assay (PEA) technology 39 coupled with next-generation sequencing. The data were expressed as Normalized Protein Expression (NPX) values. After quality control filtering, 358 proteins were retained for analysis.

Vaccine-specific antibodies (Luminex)

IgG antibodies against 36 vaccine-related antigens were measured using a custom suspension bead array on the Luminex FLEXMAP 3D platform. The panel included antigens from diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (toxin, filamentous hemagglutinin, and pertactin), Haemophilus influenzae type b, hepatitis B, poliovirus (types 1-3), rotavirus, measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines (Supplementary Table 3). Bound IgG was detected using R-phycoerythrin-conjugated anti-human IgG, and median fluorescence intensity (MFI) values were z-score normalized for cross-sample comparison.

Adverse events

Each principal investigator collected information pertaining to adverse events (AEs) or serious AEs (SAEs) on the electronic case record form (eCRF). Each AE was classified as mild, moderate, or severe and the relationship with the study product was noted as unrelated, unlikely, probable, or related. Additionally, medication type and duration of use including antibiotics and antipyretics were collected in concomitant medication reporting forms as part of the eCRF throughout the study period.

Sample size

The sample size for this trial was determined using the primary endpoint of weight gain in g/day to 4 months of age and the key secondary endpoint of sIgA concentration per dry fecal weight at 4 months. To show a non-inferiority boundary of -3g/day with a power of 80%, 88 infants per arm would be required for the primary endpoint. Based on the differences in sIgA concentrations observed across groups in a previous study and an α-level of 5%, it was estimated that 108 infants per arm would be needed to demonstrate superiority of sIgA. With the assumption of a 10% attrition rate, each group would need 120 infants (240 in total). No pre-specified interim efficacy analyses were performed.

Prespecified statistical analyses

Analyses were completed using several datasets. The intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis population consisted of all enrolled/randomized infants. The safety analysis set (SAF) comprised all infants in the ITT group who received at least one feeding of the study products. The full analysis set (FAS) included all infants from SAF except for those who could not satisfy study entry eligibility criteria or had no post-randomization data and were analyzed according to the assigned group per randomization. Lastly, the per-protocol (PP) population comprised of all FAS infants without any major departures from the protocol that could potentially influence the primary outcome. The primary endpoint of weight gain was analyzed in the FAS and PP populations while all secondary endpoints were evaluated in the FAS dataset. Safety analyses were conducted using the SAF population.

All variables were summarized using the appropriate descriptive statistics (e.g., mean, standard deviation [SD], frequency, percentage observed, etc.). The primary endpoint of weight gain was analyzed by an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model with adjustment for baseline weight, sex, and center. The key secondary endpoint of sIgA at V5 (4 months) was also analyzed using an ANCOVA model correcting for baseline value, sex, and center. Additional anthropometry measures (weight, length, head circumference, and corresponding z-scores), vital signs, GI tolerance, stool frequency and difficulty in passing stool, and stool consistency were examined using ANCOVA models at V2 (1.5 months), V3 (2 months), V4 (3 months), V5 (4 months), and V6 (6 months) with adjustment for baseline value, sex, and center. Metabolic profile and fecal markers of immune health and gut barrier function were analyzed at V3 (2 months), V5 (4 months), and V6 (6 months) while blood markers of systemic immunity were evaluated at V3 (2 months) and V5 (4 months). ANCOVA models correcting for baseline value, sex, and center were utilized for all three outcomes. Associations between microbiota and fecal biomarkers were done using Pearson correlations. Two-sided statistical tests with a significance level of 5% for nominal p-values and 10% for FDR (false discovery rate) correction were used across the different outcomes. SAS 9.4 (or higher) or R 4.1 (or higher) were used to perform statistical analyses.

Blood immune marker analyses

For Mass cytometry and Olink data, cross-sectional comparisons between feeding groups at each time point were performed using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Longitudinal analyses were conducted using linear mixed-effects models with the formula: Outcome ~ Feeding Group × Time Point + Mode of Delivery + (1|Subject), where Subject was included as a random intercept to account for repeated measures. Mode of delivery was included as a covariate given its known influence on early-life immune development. Multiple testing correction was applied using the Benjamini-Hochberg method; FDR-adjusted p<0.05 was considered statistically significant, while unadjusted p<0.05 was reported as exploratory. Effect sizes were calculated using Cohen's d with 95% confidence intervals. For vaccine-specific antibodies, cross-sectional comparisons between feeding groups were performed at V5 (4 months) using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. An integrated immune maturation metric (pseudotime) was derived by Slingshot trajectory analysis applied to the top 20% most time-varying cell populations and, separately, the top 20% most time-varying Olink plasma proteins, ordered by sampling age; resulting pseudotime values were z-scored and compared between feeding groups at each timepoint by Wilcoxon rank-sum and Mood's median tests. To identify coordinated multi-parameter signatures, weighted gene coregulation network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to a joint matrix combining the 27 manually gated CyTOF population frequencies (centered log-ratio, CLR, transformed) and all 358 Olink NPX values per sample (V1 (baseline), V3 (2 months), and V5 (4 months) pooled; n=248 samples with both modalities). A signed adjacency network was constructed using biweight midcorrelation (bicor) with a soft-thresholding power selected to approximate scale-free topology (R²≈0.8-0.9), followed by topological overlap matrix (TOM) transformation, averagelinkage hierarchical clustering, and dynamic tree cutting (hybrid method, deepSplit=4, minimum module size=6) to define co-regulation modules; modules with highly correlated eigengenes (merge height <0.10) were combined, yielding six final modules numbered by decreasing size. Each module's eigengene (first principal component of its member features) was compared between feeding groups at each timepoint using the same Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Cohen's d framework described above. Module membership (kME) -the correlation of each feature to its module's eigengene -was used to rank features within each module (Fig. 5g). Figure 1.
